candidate.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — vesicant extravasation and acute tissue injury
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize burning and swelling during vesicant infusion as possible extravasation with risk of tissue necrosis requiring prompt management.

options.A: Vesicant extravasation usually causes only transient skin discoloration without deeper tissue injury.
options.B: Burning at the site confirms a systemic allergic reaction rather than a local infusion complication.
options.C: Tissue injury is unlikely once the IV catheter is in a peripheral vein, so the infusion can continue while the site is observed.
options.D: Vesicant extravasation can cause severe local tissue injury, including necrosis, so the infusion complication requires prompt recognition and management.

candidate.rationale: NCBI StatPearls defines a vesicant as a drug that can cause tissue necrosis if it extravasates into subcutaneous tissue. Reported complications include pain, burning, stinging, erythema, sudden edema, and tissue necrosis. Management begins with stopping vesicant administration after extravasation is confirmed. Therefore burning and swelling during a vesicant infusion are urgent because serious local tissue injury can occur; D is correct.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Burning and swelling during vesicant infusion are concerning for extravasation, which can cause serious local injury including tissue necrosis and requires prompt management.
candidate.source_locator: Other Issues > Complications of Extravasation of Vesicants and Management: vesicants can cause tissue necrosis after extravasation; complications include pain, burning, stinging, erythema, sudden edema and tissue necrosis; management begins by stopping vesicant administration after confirmation.

candidate.stem: During infusion of a vesicant antineoplastic drug, the client reports burning and swelling at the IV site. Why is this finding urgent?
